It remains to show that $\displaystyle\int_{p^{-1}(x)}f\beta_m|_{p^{-1}(x)}$ converges to $\displaystyle\int_{p^{-1}(x)}f\beta|_{p^{-1}(x)}$ uniformly in $x$. By partition of unity, we may assume $(p,q)$ is injective on the support of $f$. Then $\displaystyle\int_{p^{-1}(x)}f\beta_m|_{p^{-1}(x)}$ can be viewed as an integration in $\mathbb{C}^{d-r}$. Notice that $$\left\lvert\displaystyle\int_{p^{-1}(x)}f(\beta_m-\beta)|_{p^{-1}(x)}\right\rvert\leq \sum_{i=1}^{d-r} \left\lvert\displaystyle\int_{p^{-1}(x)}f(dd^c (g_m-g)(dd^c g_m)^{d-r-i}(dd^c g)^{i-1})|_{p^{-1}(x)}\right\rvert,$$ we thus conclude the proof by the Chern--Levine--Nirenberg inequality \cite{ChernLevineNirenberg}.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{coro_null_mass}
We keep the same hypothesis as in Lemma \ref{lemm_fubini}. Let $Z\subset M$ be a closed subset. Assume for any $x\in N$, $Z\cap p^{-1}(x)$ is null with respect to $\beta$ on $p^{-1}(x)$. Then $Z$ is null with respect to $\beta\wedge p^*\alpha$
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
We may assume $Z$ is compact. By an approximation of $Z$ we mean a family $(f_n)_{n\ge1}$ of continuous functions with compact support on $M$ such that $f_n=1$ on $Z$, and $(f_n)_{n\ge 1}$ decrease pointwise to $0$ outside $Z$. We can always construct such an approximation.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
Applying the dominated convergence theorem, the signed measure $(\beta\wedge p^*\alpha)(Z)$ of $Z$ equals the limit of $\displaystyle\int_{M}f_n\beta\wedge p^*\alpha$ as $n\to\infty$. For any $x\in N$, $(f_n|_{p^{-1}(x)})_{n\ge1}$ is an approximation of $Z\cap p^{-1}(x)$. So $\displaystyle\int_{p^{-1}(x)}f_n\beta|_{p^{-1}(x)}\to0$ as $n\rightarrow\infty$, since $Z\cap p^{-1}(x)$ is null with respect to $\beta$. Using Lemma \ref{lemm_fubini}, we obtain that
$$\int_{M}f_n\beta\wedge p^*\alpha=\int_N\Big(\int_{p^{-1}(x)}f_n\beta|_{p^{-1}(x)}\Big)\alpha(x).$$
Recall that $\beta=(dd^c g)^{d-r}$, we can decompose $\beta$ into the positive part and the negative part.
By applying the monotone convergence theorem to both parts respectively,
$$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\int_N\Big(\int_{p^{-1}(x)}f_n\beta|_{p^{-1}(x)}\Big)\alpha(x)=\int_N\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\Big(\int_{p^{-1}(x)}f_n\beta|_{p^{-1}(x)}\Big)\alpha(x)=0,$$
which concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{measure}
Let $U\subset{\mathcal X}^{\mathrm{sm}}(\mathbb{C})$ be the $I$-non-degeneracy locus. Denote by $j:U\cap{\mathcal G}_{I,\mathbb S^1}\to{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})$ the inclusion map. Then
$$c_1(\overline L)^rc_1(\overline M_I)^{\lvert I\rvert}=j_*(c_1(\overline L)^r\omega_I^{\lvert I\rvert}).$$
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
Since ${\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})\setminus{\mathcal X}^{\mathrm{sm}}(\mathbb{C})$ is pluripolar, it is null with respect to $c_1(\overline L)^rc_1(\overline M_I)^{\lvert I\rvert}$. Let $V\subset{\mathcal X}^{\mathrm{sm}}(\mathbb{C})$ be the open subset where the maximal abelian Betti rank $2r$ is attained. Then the smooth $(r,r)$-form $c_1(\overline L)^r$ vanishes outside $V$. Thus, ${\mathcal X}^{\mathrm{sm}}(\mathbb{C})\setminus V$ is also null.

Note that for any $x\in U$, $$\mathrm{rank}_\mathbb{R}(d(\widetilde{b_{\mathrm{ab}},b_I})|_{\widetilde{{\mathcal X}}}))_{\widetilde x}=2\dim{\mathcal X}$$ implies that $$\mathrm{rank}_\mathbb{R}(d(\widetilde b_{\mathrm{ab}}|_{\widetilde {\mathcal X}}))_{\widetilde x}=2r.$$ Indeed, 
\begin{align*}2\dim{\mathcal X}&=\mathrm{rank}_\mathbb{R}(d(\widetilde{b_{\mathrm{ab}},b_I})|_{\widetilde{{\mathcal X}}}))_{\widetilde x}\\&\le\mathrm{rank}_\mathbb{R}(d(\widetilde b_{\mathrm{ab}}|_{\widetilde {\mathcal X}}))_{\widetilde x}+\mathrm{rank}_\mathbb{R}(d(\widetilde b_{I}|_{\widetilde {\mathcal X}}))_{\widetilde x}\\&\le 2r+2(\lvert I\rvert)=2\dim{\mathcal X}.
\end{align*}
So the equalities hold. We get $U\subset V$.

For any point $y\in V$, we may take an open neighborhood $M\subset V$ whose closure $\overline M$ is compact and simply connected.                                                                                                              
Since $b_{\mathrm{ab}}$ has constant rank $2r$ near $y$, after shrinking $M$, $b_{\mathrm{ab}}$ factors through a submersion $p:M\to N$ and an immersion $N\to(\mathbb{R}/{\mathbb Z})^{2g}$ of real manifolds. Recall that $c_1(\overline L)$ is a pull-back along $b_{\mathrm{ab}}$ by \eqref{eq_currents_pull_back_via_betti} and \eqref{eq_first_Chern_form_pullback}. So there is a $(2r)$-form $\alpha$ on $N$ such that $p^*\alpha=c_1(\overline L)^r$.

\begin{equation}\label{eq_cd_real_manifolds}\begin{tikzcd}
	M & {(\mathbb{R}/{\mathbb Z})^{2g}} \\
	N
	\arrow["{b_{\mathrm{ab}}}", from=1-1, to=1-2]
	\arrow["p"', from=1-1, to=2-1]
	\arrow[from=2-1, to=1-2]
\end{tikzcd}\end{equation}


                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   
Notice that the restriction of $b_{I}$ on $p^{-1}(p(y))=b_{\mathrm{ab}}^{-1}b_{\mathrm{ab}}(y)\cap M$ is holomorphic by the formula \eqref{eq_Betti_map}.
For any continuous function $f$ with compact support on $M$, by Lemma \ref{lemm_fubini},
$$\int_Mfc_1(\overline L)^rc_1(\overline M_I)^{\lvert I\rvert}=\int_N\Big(\int_{p^{-1}(x)}fc_1(\overline M_I|_{p^{-1}(x)})^{\lvert I\rvert}\Big)\alpha.$$

For $x\in N$, $\dim (b_{I}((V\setminus U)\cap p^{-1}(x))<\lvert I\rvert$. Hence $(V\setminus U)\cap p^{-1}(x)$ is null with respect to $c_1(\overline M_I)^{\lvert I\rvert}$ again by the holomorphicity \eqref{eq_Betti_map}. So $(V\setminus U)\cap M$ is null with respect to $c_1(\overline L)^rc_1(\overline M_I)^{\lvert I\rvert}$ due to Corollary \ref{coro_null_mass}. By taking a countable collection of $M$'s that covers $V$, we see that $V\setminus U$ is so.

Assume $M\subset U$ in the sequel. 
Since $p|_{U\cap{\mathcal G}_{I,\mathbb S^1}}$ is submersive onto $N$, by the Fubini theorem for smooth forms,
$$\int_{M\cap{\mathcal G}_{I,\mathbb S^1}}(j^*f)c_1(\overline L)^r\omega_I^{\lvert I\rvert}=\int_N\Big(\int_{p^{-1}(x)\cap{\mathcal G}_{I,\mathbb S^1}}(j^*f)\omega_I^{\lvert I\rvert}\Big)\alpha.$$

It remains to prove
$$c_1(\overline M_I|_{p^{-1}(x)})^{\lvert I\rvert}=j_*(\omega_{I}|_{p^{-1}(x)\cap{\mathcal G}_{I,\mathbb S^1}}^{\lvert I\rvert}).$$
Recall that $b_I^*$ commutes with $dd^c$ due to holomorphicity, and the Green function of $\overline M_I$ is the pull-back of $\sum_{i\in I}|\log|z_i||$. So we only need to prove
$$(\sum_{i=1}^ndd^c|\log|z_i||)^n=j_*(\sum_{i=1}^np_i^*\omega_{\mathbb S^1})^n.$$
on $(\mathbb{C}^\times)^{n}$. The case that $n=1$ can be verified by direct calculation. We then conclude the proof by induction on $n$.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{theorem_I_non_deg_integral}
Let ${\mathcal X}\subset{\mathcal G}$ be a subvariety. Let $2r$ be its abelian Betti rank. Let $I\subset\{1,2,\dots,t\}$ be a $(\dim{\mathcal X}-r)$-element subset. Then ${\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})$ is $I$-non-degenerate if and only if
$$\int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline L)^{r}c_1(\overline M_I)^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}>0.$$
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{remark_I_non_deg_equiv_non_deg}
For completeness, we remark that ${\mathcal X}$ is non-degenerate if and only if
$$\int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline L)^{r}c_1(\overline M)^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}>0.$$
This can be derived from the following two facts: \begin{enumerate}
    \item ${\mathcal X}$ is non-degenerate if and only if it is $I$-non-degenerate for some $I$ with $\lvert I\rvert=\dim \mathcal X-r$;
    \item $$\int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline L)^{r}c_1(\overline M)^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}>0$$
if and only if
$$\int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline L)^{r}c_1(\overline M_I)^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}>0$$
for some $I$.
\end{enumerate}
 To see the second fact, note that the proof of Theorem \ref{measure} actually implies that each term
$$c_1(\overline L)^rc_1(\overline M_{\{i_1\}})c_1(\overline M_{\{i_2\}})\cdots c_1(\overline M_{\{i_{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}\}})$$
in the expansion of $c_1(\overline L)^{r}c_1(\overline M)^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}$ is a non-negative measure on ${\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})$. So the strict positivity of total measure is equivalent to that of some term.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
By Theorem \ref{measure}, if
$$\int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline L)^{r}c_1(\overline M_I)^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}>0,$$
then ${\mathcal X}$ is $I$-non-degenerate.

Conversely, assume that ${\mathcal X}$ is $I$-non-degenerate. Let $x$ be an $I$-non-degenerate point. There exists a simply connected open neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contained in the $I$-non-degeneracy locus. By fixing a lifting, we get the Betti map $(b_I,b_{\mathrm{ab}}):U\to(\mathbb{C}^\times)^{\lvert I\rvert}\times (\mathbb{R}^{2g}/\mathbb{Z}^{2g})$. Similarly as in \eqref{eq_cd_real_manifolds}, the image $(b_I,b_\mathrm{ab})(U)$ contains a real  manifold $M$ around $(b_I,b_\mathrm{ab})(x)$, with a submersion $M\rightarrow N\subset\mathbb{R}^{2g}/\mathbb{Z}^{2g}$ of real manifolds. We may assume that $M$ is open in $ (\mathbb{C}^\times)^{\lvert I\rvert}\times N$.

We first consider the case that $x\in {\mathcal G}_{I,\mathbb S^1}$. Since the map $$\lambda:(\mathbb{C}^\times)^{\lvert I\rvert}\rightarrow (\mathbb{R}_{>0})^{\lvert I\rvert}, (z_1,\dots, z_{{\lvert I\rvert}})\mapsto (\lvert z_1\rvert,\dots, \lvert z_{{\lvert I\rvert}}\rvert)$$ is open, $\lambda(M)$ contains an open real submanifold of $\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{\lvert I\rvert}$ around $\lambda((b_I,b_\mathrm{ab})(x))=1$. Therefore $(\lambda\circ(b_I,b_\mathrm{ab}))^{-1}(1)\subset U\cap \mathcal G_{I,\mathbb S^1}$ contains an real manifold near $x$, and $c_1(\overline L)^r\omega_I^{\lvert I\rvert}$ is a non-vanishing smooth top form on this manifold. So the integral is strictly positive.

In general, we may take a point $s\in\mathbb{G}_m^{\lvert I\rvert}(\mathbb{C})$ such that $b_I(U)+s$ intersects $(\mathbb S^1)^{\lvert I\rvert}$. Denote by $t_s:{\mathcal G}\to{\mathcal G}$ the translation by $s$. Then $t_s({\mathcal X})$ has an $I$-non-degenerate point contained in ${\mathcal G}_{I,\mathbb S^1}$. Thus,
$$(\widetilde L|_{t_s({\mathcal X})}^{r}\cdot\widetilde M_I|_{t_s({\mathcal X})}^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r})=\int_{t_s({\mathcal X})(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline L)^{r}c_1(\overline M_I)^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}>0.$$
First note that $c_1(\overline L)$ is translation invariant. The Green function of $t_s^*\overline M_I-\overline M_I$ is
$$\sum_{i\in I}(|-\log|s_ib_{\mathrm{tor}}(\cdot)||-|-\log|b_{\mathrm{tor}}(\cdot)||),$$
where $s_i$ is the $i$-th component of $s$. The triangular inequality
$$\Big\lvert\big\lvert-\log\lvert s_iz\rvert\big\rvert -\big\lvert-\log\lvert z\rvert\big\rvert\Big\rvert\le\big\lvert-\log\lvert s_i\rvert\big\rvert.$$
implies this Green function is bounded. By \cite[Theorem 3.6.4]{YuanZhang}, $t_s^*\widetilde M_I=\widetilde M_I$. Therefore,
$$\int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline L)^{r}c_1(\overline M_I)^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}=(\widetilde L|_{{\mathcal X}}^{r}\cdot\widetilde M_I|_{{\mathcal X}}^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r})=(\widetilde L|_{t_s({\mathcal X})}^{r}\cdot\widetilde M_I|_{t_s({\mathcal X})}^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r})>0.$$
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- proposition-12: body_md -->
\label{big}
Assume that ${\mathcal X}\subset{\mathcal G}$ is $I$-non-degenerate. Let $\overline H$ be a nef adelic line bundle on $S$. Then there is a positive integers $n$ and a positive constant $e>0$ such that for any positive integer $m$ large enough,
$$(m^2n\overline L+m\overline M_I-\pi_{\mathcal G/S}^*\overline H+\overline{\mathcal O}(e))|_{\mathcal X}$$
is big.
<!-- end proposition-12 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
By Proposition \ref{integrable} there is a positive integer $n$ and a nef adelic line bundle $\overline H'$ on $S$ such that the adelic line bundle
$$\overline Q_1=n\overline L+\overline M_I+\pi_{\mathcal G/S}^*\overline H'$$
on ${\mathcal G}$ is nef. Thus so is $\overline Q_m=[m]^*\overline Q_1=m^2n\overline L+m\overline M_I+\overline H'$

Since $\overline Q_m+\overline{\mathcal{O}}(e)$ and $\overline H+\overline H'$ are both nef, after applying the arithmetic Siu's inequality \eqref{eq_Siu_inequality},
\begin{align*}
&\kern-1em \widehat{\mathrm{vol}}((m^2n\overline L+m\overline M_I-\overline H+\overline{\mathcal{O}}(e))|_{\mathcal X})\\
=&\ \widehat{\mathrm{vol}}((\overline Q_m+\overline{\mathcal{O}}(e)-\overline H-\overline H')|_{\mathcal X})\\
\ge&\ ((\overline Q_m+\overline{\mathcal{O}}(e))|_{\mathcal X})^{\dim{\mathcal X}+1}-(\dim{\mathcal X}+1)((\overline Q_m+\overline{\mathcal O}(e))|_{\mathcal X}^{\dim{\mathcal X}}\cdot(\overline H+\overline H')|_{\mathcal X})\\
=&\ (\overline Q_m|_{\mathcal X})^{\dim{\mathcal X}+1}+e(\dim{\mathcal X}+1)(\widetilde Q_m|_{{\mathcal X}}^{\dim{\mathcal X}})\\
&\ -(\dim{\mathcal X}+1)\Big(\big(\overline Q_m|_{\mathcal X}^{\dim{\mathcal X}}\cdot(\overline H+\overline H')|_{\mathcal X}\big)+e\dim{\mathcal X}\big(\widetilde Q_m|_{{\mathcal X}}^{\dim{\mathcal X}-1}\cdot(\widetilde H+\widetilde H')|_{\mathcal X}\big)\Big)\\
=&\ e(\dim{\mathcal X}+1)\Big(\big(\widetilde Q_m|_{{\mathcal X}}\big)^{\dim{\mathcal X}}-\dim{\mathcal X}\big(\widetilde Q_m|_{{\mathcal X}}^{\dim{\mathcal X}-1}\cdot(\widetilde H+\widetilde H')|_{\mathcal X}\big)\Big)\\
&\ +(\overline Q_m|_{\mathcal X})^{\dim{\mathcal X}+1}-(\dim{\mathcal X}+1)(\overline Q_m|_{\mathcal X}^{\dim{\mathcal X}}\cdot(\overline H+\overline H')|_{\mathcal X})
\end{align*}
This lower bound is a linear function in $e$. Once we have
$$(\widetilde Q_m|_{{\mathcal X}})^{\dim{\mathcal X}}-\dim{\mathcal X}(\widetilde Q_m|_{{\mathcal X}}^{\dim{\mathcal X}-1}\cdot(\widetilde H+\widetilde H')|_{\mathcal X})>0,$$
then $(m^2n\overline L+m\overline M_I-\overline H+\overline{\mathcal{O}}(e))|_{\mathcal X}$ is big for $e$ large enough. It remains to prove the above inequality holds for some large $m$.

We analyze the asymptotic behavior as $m\to\infty$. Since $2r$ is the Betti rank of $\pi({\mathcal X})$, we have
$$c_1(\overline L|_{\mathcal X})^{r+1}=0.$$
So
\begin{align*}
&\ (\widetilde Q_m|_{{\mathcal X}}^{\dim{\mathcal X}})-\dim{\mathcal X}(\widetilde Q_m|_{{\mathcal X}}^{\dim{\mathcal X}-1}\cdot(\widetilde H+\widetilde H')|_{\mathcal X})\\
=&\ \int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline Q_m)^{\dim{\mathcal X}}-\dim{\mathcal X}\int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline Q_m)^{\dim{\mathcal X}-1}c_1(\overline H+\overline H')\\
=&\ m^{\dim{\mathcal X}+r}\binom{\dim{\mathcal X}}{r}\int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline L)^r\cdot c_1(\overline M_I)^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}+O(m^{\dim{\mathcal X}+r-1}).  
\end{align*}
We conclude the proof.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{weak_bogomolov}
We keep the same hypothesis as in Proposition \ref{big}. Then
$$\{x\in {\mathcal X}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}):\widehat{h}_I(x)\le\epsilon h_{\overline H}(\pi_{\mathcal G/S}(x))-\delta\}$$
is not Zariski dense in ${\mathcal X}$ for some positive constants $\epsilon$, $\delta>0$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
By the bigness, some positive multiple of $(m^2n\overline L+m\overline M_I-\pi_{\mathcal G/S}^*\overline H+\overline{\mathcal O}(e))|_{\mathcal X}$ admits an effective section $s$. Then
$$h_{m^2n\overline L+m\overline M_I-\pi_{\mathcal G/S}^*\overline H'+\overline{\mathcal O}(e)}(\cdot)\ge0$$
on $({\mathcal X}\setminus|\mathrm{div}(s)|)(\overline\mathbb{Q})$. Since
\begin{align*}
    h_{m^2n\overline L+m\overline M_I-\pi_{\mathcal G/S}^*\overline H+\overline{\mathcal O}(e)}(x)&=h_{m^2n\overline L+m\overline M_I}(x)-h_{\overline H}(\pi_{\mathcal G/S}(x))+e\\&\le m^2n\widehat{h}_I(x)-h_{\overline H}(\pi_{\mathcal G/S}(x))+e,
\end{align*}
the statement holds for $\epsilon=m^{-2}n^{-1},\delta=m^{-2}n^{-1}e$.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- theorem-14: body_md -->
\label{theorem_equidistribution}
Let ${\mathcal X}\subset{\mathcal G}$ be a closed subvariety. Let $x_i\in{\mathcal X}\ (n=1,2\dots)$ be a generic sequence of closed points. If ${\mathcal X}$ is $I$-non-degenerate and
$$\lim_{i\to\infty}\widehat{h}_I(x_i)=0,$$
then the sequence $(x_i)$ equidistributes to
$$\frac{c_1(\overline L|_{{\mathcal X}})^rc_1(\overline M_I|_{\mathcal X})^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}}{\displaystyle\int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline L)^rc_1(\overline M_I)^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}}.$$
<!-- end theorem-14 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Take $n$ and $e$ as in Proposition \ref{big}. Note that $nm^2\overline L+m\overline M_I+
\overline H$ is nef for all $m$. Denote $\overline N=(n\overline L+\overline M_I)|_{\mathcal X}$. Take the $\mathbb{Q}$-adelic line bundle
$$\overline Q_m=\Big(\frac{n}{2}\overline L+\frac{1}{2m}\overline M_I+\frac{1}{2m^2}\overline H-\frac{1}{2m^2}\overline{\mathcal{O}}(e)\Big)\Big|_{\mathcal X}$$
on ${\mathcal X}$. We show that $\overline Q_m$ is a \emph{semipositive approximation} of $\overline N$ for $m$ large enough in the sense of \cite[Definition 8.10]{BS} and the sequence satisfies the conditions of \cite[Theorem 8.11]{BS}. Once this is done, the sequence $(x_i)$ equidistributes to the weak limit
$$\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{c_1(\overline Q_m)^{\dim{\mathcal X}}}{\displaystyle\int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline Q_m)^{\dim{\mathcal X}}}.$$
Since
\begin{align*}
c_1(\overline Q_m|_{\mathcal X})^{\dim{\mathcal X}}&=m^{-\dim{\mathcal X}+r}\binom{\dim{\mathcal X}}{r}\frac{n^r}{2^{\dim{\mathcal X}}}c_1(\overline L|_{\mathcal X})^rc_1(\overline M_I|_{\mathcal X})^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}\\
&+O(m^{-\dim{\mathcal X}+r-1}),
\end{align*}
we get the equilibrum measure
$$\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{c_1(\overline Q_m)^{\dim{\mathcal X}}}{\displaystyle\int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline Q_m)^{\dim{\mathcal X}}}=\frac{c_1(\overline L|_{\mathcal X})^rc_1(\overline M_I|_{\mathcal X})^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}}{\displaystyle\int_{{\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})}c_1(\overline L)^rc_1(\overline M_I)^{\dim{\mathcal X}-r}}.$$

We first check that $(\overline Q_m)_{m\ge1}$ is a semipositive approximation of $\overline N$. Note that the birational map is taken to be the identity map of ${\mathcal X}$. So we only need:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(i)]$\overline Q_m$ is semipositive;
    \item[(ii)]$\widetilde Q_m$ is big;
    \item[(iii)]$\overline N-\overline Q_m$ is pseudo-effective. 
\end{enumerate}
For (i), since $\overline Q_m+\frac1{2m^2}\overline{\mathcal{O}}(e)$ is nef, $\overline Q_m$ is semipositive. By Proposition \ref{big}, both
\begin{equation}\label{eq_decompose_Qm}
    \overline Q_m+\frac1{m^2}\overline{\mathcal{O}}(e)=\frac{1}{2m^2}(m^2n\overline L+m\overline M_I-\pi_{\mathcal G/S}^*\overline H+\overline{\mathcal O}(e))|_{\mathcal X}+\frac{1}{m^2}\pi_{\mathcal G/S}^*\overline H|_{\mathcal X}
\end{equation}
and
$$\overline N-\overline Q_m=\frac{1}{2m^2}(m^2n\overline L+m\overline M_I-\pi_{\mathcal G/S}^*\overline H+\overline{\mathcal O}(e))|_{\mathcal X}$$
are big. This implies (ii) and (iii) for $m$ large enough.

Take
$$r_n=\sup\{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}:\widetilde Q_m-\lambda\widetilde N\mathrm{\ is\ big}\}.$$
It remains to verify the following conditions of \cite[Theorem 8.11]{BS}:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(1)]$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{1}{r_n}\left(\mathrm{ess}(\overline N)-\frac{\overline Q_m^{\dim{\mathcal X}+1}}{(\dim{\mathcal X}+1)\widetilde Q_m^{\dim{\mathcal X}}}\right)=0;$$
    \item[(2)]$$\sup_n\frac{\mathrm{ess}(\overline N)-\mathrm{abs}(\overline Q_m)}{r_n}<\infty.$$
\end{enumerate}
Since
$$\widetilde Q_m-\frac1{4m}\widetilde N=\frac{2m-1}{4m}\widetilde L+\frac{1}{4m}\widetilde M_I+\frac{1}{2m^2}\widetilde H'$$
is big, $r_n\ge\frac1{4m}$. By the assumption that $\widehat{h}_I(x_i)\to0$, $\mathrm{ess}(\widetilde N)=0$. Since $(x_i)$ is generic, by Corollary \ref{weak_bogomolov}, for $i$ large enough, $h({\mathcal X}_{\pi_{\mathcal G/S}(x_i)})\le\epsilon_1^{-1}\widehat h(x_i)+\epsilon_1^{-1}\delta$. Therefore,
\begin{align*}
    -\frac e{2m^2}\le \mathrm{abs}(\overline Q_m)&\le\frac{\overline Q_m^{\dim{\mathcal X}+1}}{(\dim{\mathcal X}+1)\widetilde Q_m^{\dim{\mathcal X}}}\le \mathrm{ess}(\overline Q_m)\\&\le\liminf_{i\to\infty}h_{\overline Q_m}(x_i)\le\liminf_{i\to\infty}h_{\frac1{2m^2}\overline H}(\pi_{\mathcal G/S}(x_i))\le\frac{\epsilon^{-1}\delta}{2m^2},
\end{align*}
where the second and the third inequality are due to \eqref{eq_fundamental} and \eqref{eq_fundamental2} respectively, and the fifth inequality is due \eqref{eq_decompose_Qm} and $\lim \widehat h_{I}(x)=0$.
Therefore (1) and (2) follow.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- theorem-15: body_md -->
\label{bogomolov}
There exist positive constants $c_1(g+t,d)$, $c_2(g+t,d)>0$ satisfying the property as follows. Let $G$ be a principally polarized semiabelian variety over $\overline\mathbb{Q}$ of dimension $g+t$ with a level-$4$ structure. Let $X\subset G$ be a closed subvariety of degree $d$, such that $X$ generates the abelian quotient $A$. Then there is a reduced closed subscheme $Z\subset X$ of degree at most $c_1(g+t,d)$ such that
$$\#\{x\in X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q}):\widehat{h}(x)\le c_2(g+t,d)h([X])\}\subset Z(\overline\mathbb{Q})$$
where the definition of $h([X])$ will be given in \eqref{eq_modular_height}.
<!-- end theorem-15 -->
<!-- proposition-13: body_md -->
\label{hilbert}
    For any algebraically closed field $K$ of characteristic $0$, a principally polarized semiabelian variety $G$ over $K$, and a closed subvariety $X\subset G$ of degree $d$, 
    after fixing a level-$4$ structure on $G$,
    there exists a unique $K$-point $i_X\in\mathrm{Hilb}_{g,t,d}^\circ$ such that $X=i_X^*\mathfrak X$.
    We denote the point $i_X$ as $[X].$
<!-- end proposition-13 -->
<!-- theorem-16: body_md -->
\label{relative}
Let $S$ be a subvariety of $\mathrm{Hilb}_{g,t,d}^\circ,$  $\mathcal G:=S\times_{(\mathcal A_g^\vee)^{[t]}} \mathcal P_{g,t}^\times$, and $\mathcal X:=\mathfrak X_S.$ Let $\overline\eta$ be the geometric generic point of $S$. Assume that 
for every $s\in S$, ${\mathcal X}_s$ generates the abelian quotient $\mathcal A_s$.
Then either ${\mathcal X}_s^\circ$ is empty for every $s\in S(\overline\mathbb{Q})$, or there is a positive integer $n$ and a positive number $\epsilon>0$ such that
$$\{x\in \mathcal X^{[n]}(\overline\mathbb{Q}):\widehat{h}(x)\le\epsilon h([\mathcal X_s]), x\in \mathcal X^n_s\}$$
is not Zariski dense in $\mathcal X^{[n]}$.
<!-- end theorem-16 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
To get Theorem \ref{bogomolov}, consider the subset 
$$\mathrm{Hilb}^{\circ, \mathrm{gen}}_{g,t,d}:=\{[X]\in \mathrm{Hilb}^\circ_{g,t,d}\,:\, X\text{ generates }A\}$$
where $A$ is the abelian quotient of the ambient semiabelian variety $G$ of $X$. This is a closed subset of $\mathrm{Hilb}^\circ_{g,t,d}$ due to \cite[Lemma 3.5]{GGK}. Note that this closedness may fail if we replace ``generating $A$" with ``generating $G$".

After letting $S$ run over irreducible components of $\mathrm{Hilb}^{\circ, \mathrm{gen}}_{g,t,d}$ equipped with reduced scheme structures, it suffices to show that for any $s\in S(\overline\mathbb{Q})$, there is a reduced subscheme $Z_s\subset{\mathcal X}_s$ of degree at most $c_1({\mathcal X}/S)$ such that
$$\#\{x\in {\mathcal X}_s^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\,:\,\widehat{h}(x)\le c_2({\mathcal X}/S)h([{\mathcal X}_s])\}\subset Z_s(\overline\mathbb{Q})$$
for some positive constants $c_1({\mathcal X}/S)$, $c_2({\mathcal X}/S)>0$. 

If every ${\mathcal X}_s^\circ$ is empty, there is nothing to prove. Assume 
$$\{x\in \mathcal X^{[n]}(\overline {\mathbb{Q}})\,:\,\widehat{h}(x)\le\epsilon h([{\mathcal X}_s], x\in \mathcal X^n_s\}\subset{\mathcal Z}$$
for some $\epsilon>0$, and a reduced closed subscheme ${\mathcal Z}\subsetneq\mathcal X^{[n]}$. We prove the statement by induction on $\dim S$.

Consider the Zariski closure $\overline{\mathcal Z}$ (resp. $\overline{\mathcal X^{[n]}}=\overline{\mathcal X}^{[n]} $) of $\mathcal Z$ (resp. $\mathcal X^{[n]}$) in $\overline{\mathcal G^{[n]}}=\overline{\mathcal G}^{[n]}$. 
Since $\overline {\mathcal X^{[n]}}$ is irreducible, we may enlarge $\mathcal Z$ so that $\overline{\mathcal Z}\subsetneq \overline {\mathcal X^{[n]}}$ is equidimensional.

There is an open subvariety $U\subset S$ such that $\overline {\mathcal Z}_U$ is flat and equidimensional over $U$. In particular, for $s\in U$, $\overline Z_s\subsetneq \overline{\mathcal X_s^{[n]}}$ (the ``$\subsetneq$" is due to dimension reason) are of constant degree. Then \cite[Lemma 4.3]{GGK} implies the statement over $U$\footnote{For a sufficiently large $\ell$, $\ell(L+M)$ is relatively very ample over $S$. Here we substitute $L$ and $\Sigma$ in the original statement of \cite[Lemma 4.3]{GGK}, with $\ell(L+M)$ and $\{x\in {\mathcal X}_s^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\,:\,\widehat{h}(x)\le c_2({\mathcal X}/S)h([{\mathcal X}_s])\}$ respectively. For a closed subvariety $X'\subsetneq X$, ${\mathrm{deg}}_{L+M}(X')\leq {\mathrm{deg}}_{\ell(L+M)}(X')$, hence we obtained the statement as desired.}. Decompose the complement $S\setminus U$ into closed subvarieties $S_1,\dots,S_m$. 
The induction hypothesis implies the statement over them. We thus conclude the proof by setting
$$c_1({\mathcal X}/S):=\max\{c_1({\mathcal X}_U/U),c_1({\mathcal X}_{S_1}/S_1),\dots,c_1({\mathcal X}_{S_m}/S_m)\}$$
and
$$c_2({\mathcal X}/S):=\min\{c_2({\mathcal X}_U/U),c_2({\mathcal X}_{S_1}/S_1),\dots,c_2({\mathcal X}_{S_m}/S_m)\}.$$
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
Let $S$ be a (irreducible) subvariety of $\mathrm{Hilb}_{g,t,d}^\circ$, and $\mathcal X:=\mathfrak X_S$. Then for $m$ large enough, $\mathcal X^{[m]}\to\iota^{[m]}(\mathcal X^{[m]})$ is generically finite.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lemma_non_deg_indices}
Let $(\mathcal G,\mathcal X)$ and $(\mathcal G',\mathcal X')$ be two two pairs over $S$ as in the begining of this section. Assume $x\in\mathcal X^{\mathrm{sm}}(\mathbb C)$ is an $I$-non-degenerate point for some index set of toric part of $\mathcal G$. Let $I'$ be the index set for the whole toric part of $\mathcal G'$. Then any smooth point $x'\in(x\times_S\mathcal X')^\mathrm{sm}(\mathbb C)$ on the fiber over $x$ is an $(I\sqcup I')$-non-degenerate point.

In particular, if $\mathcal X$ is $I$-non-degenerate, then $\mathcal X\times_S\mathcal X'$ is $(I\sqcup I')$-non-degenerate.
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
Denote by $Y=x\times_S\mathcal X'$ the fiber over $x$. There is a short exact sequence of tangent spaces:
$$0\longrightarrow T_{x'}Y\longrightarrow T_{x'}(\mathcal X\times_S\mathcal X')\longrightarrow T_{x}\mathcal X\longrightarrow0.$$
We need to show the $(I\sqcup I')$-th Betti map in injective on $T_{x'}(\mathcal X\times_S\mathcal X')$. By the hypothesis on $\mathcal X$, the $I$-th Betti map is injective on $T_x\mathcal X$. Thus, if some tangent vector is killed by the differential of the $(I\sqcup I')$-th Betti map, it must lie in $T_{x'}Y$. However, $Y$ is contained in a single semiabelian variety. So the $I'$-th Betti map is injective on $T_{x'}Y$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
We may and do assume that $\mathcal X$ is non-degenerate after replace $\mathcal X$ by $\mathcal X^{[m]}$ for some $m\gg 0.$

We denote by $\overline L^{\boxtimes n}$ (resp. $\overline M^{\boxtimes n}$) the fiberwise box product $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i^*\overline L$ (resp. $\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{n}p_i^*\overline M$) where $p_i:\mathcal G^{[n]}\rightarrow \mathcal G$ is the $i$-th projection.

Now we only need to prove (BC2), which is equivalent to $$\mathrm{ess}((\overline L+\overline M)^{\boxtimes n}|_{\mathcal X^{[n]}})>0$$ for some positive integer $n$.

Assume the contrary. Consider the fiberwise \emph{Faltings--Zhang map}
\begin{align*}
    \alpha_n:\mathcal G^{[n]}&\longrightarrow \mathcal G^{[n-1]},\\
    (x_1,\dots, x_n)&\longmapsto (x_1-x_2,\dots, x_{n-1}-x_n).
\end{align*}
By the proof of \cite[Lemma 3.1]{Zhang98BC}, we can take an $n$ large enough such that $\mathcal X^{[n]}\rightarrow \alpha_n(\mathcal X^{[n]})$ is generically finite.

Take a generic sequence $(x_i)$ in $\mathcal X^{[n+1]}$ such that $\widehat h(x_i)\to 0\ (n\to\infty)$. Hence $\widehat h_I(x_i)\to 0\ (n\to\infty)$ for any set $I$ of indices.

Let $x\in{\mathcal X}^\mathrm{sm}(\mathbb{C})\cap{\mathcal G}_{I,\mathbb S^1}$ be an $I$-non-degenerate point where ${\mathcal X}(\mathbb{C})$ is smooth over $S(\mathbb{C})$. Then by Lemma \ref{lemma_non_deg_indices}, $(x,x,\dots,x)\in({\mathcal X}^{[n+1]})^\mathrm{sm}(\mathbb{C})\cap(\mathcal G^{[n+1]})_{I_1,{\mathbb S^1}}$ is $I_1$-non-degenerate for some $I_1$. Moreover, $\mathcal X\times_S\alpha_n(\mathcal X^{[n]})$ is $I_2$-non-degenerate for some $I_2$.

We denote that $\alpha=\mathrm{id}_{\mathcal G}\times_S \alpha_n.$
Applying Theorem \ref{theorem_equidistribution} to $(x_i)$ in $\mathcal X^{[n+1]}$ and $(x_1,\alpha(x_i))$ in $\mathcal X\times_S\alpha_n(\mathcal X^{[n]})$ respectively. 
Since $\alpha_*\delta_{x_i}=\delta_{\alpha(x_i)}$, we get
$$\alpha_*\mu_{I_1}=\mu_{I_2},$$
where $\mu_{I_1}$ (resp. $\mu_{I_2}$) is the equilibrum measure on $\mathcal X^{[n+1]}(\mathbb{C})$ (resp. $(\mathcal X\times_S\alpha_n(\mathcal X^{[n]}))(\mathbb{C})$).

Let $U_1$ (resp. $U_2$) be the $I_1$-non-degeneracy (resp. $I_2$-non-degeneracy) locus of $\mathcal X^{[n+1]}$ (resp. $\mathcal X\times_S\alpha_n(\mathcal X^{[n]})$).
Put $\Sigma_1:=(\mathcal G^{[n+1]})_{I_1,{\mathbb S^1}}$ and $\Sigma_2:=(\mathcal G^{[n]})_{I_2,{\mathbb S^1}}.$
Then by Theorem \ref{measure}, \begin{equation}\label{eq_measure_to_form}
    \mu_{I_1}|_{U_1}=\omega_1|_{U_1\cap\Sigma_1}\text{ (resp. }\mu_{I_2}|_{U_2}=\omega_2|_{U_2\cap \Sigma_2})
\end{equation} for some smooth non-vanishing form $\omega_1$ (resp. $\omega_2$) on $\Sigma_1$ (resp. $\Sigma_2$).

Let $V$ be a Zariski open subset such that $\alpha|_V:V\to\alpha(V)$ is finite and étale. Since $(\mathcal X^{[n]}\setminus V)(\mathbb{C})$ (resp. $(\alpha(\mathcal X^{[n]})\setminus \alpha(V))(\mathbb{C})$) is polaripolar, thus null under $\mu_1$ ({resp.} $\mu_2$). Hence $\mu_1$ is null outside $W=V\cap U_1\cap\alpha^{-1}(U_2)$. By comparing the support of $\alpha_*(\mu_1|_W)$ and $\mu_2|_{\alpha(W)}$, we get $\alpha(W\cap\Sigma_1)\subset\Sigma_2$. 

Moreover, by \eqref{eq_measure_to_form}, we can interpret the relation of measure pushforward as smooth forms pulling-back, that is, $$\alpha^*\omega_2=\omega_1$$ on $W\cap\Sigma_1$. 

Since $U_1\cap\Sigma_1$ is a real analytic manifold due to the definition of being $I_1$-non-degenerate, and the complement of $W$ in $(\mathcal X^{[n+1]})^{\mathrm{sm}}(\mathbb{C})$ is real analytic, we get that $W\cap\Sigma_1$ is dense in $U_1\cap\Sigma_1$. Thus, $\alpha(U_1\cap\Sigma_1)\subset\Sigma_2$ and $\alpha^*\omega_2=\omega_1$ at $(x,x,\dots,x)\in U_1\cap \Sigma_1$. However, $\alpha^*\omega_2$ vanishes at $(x,x,\dots,x)$ (which can be obtained by calculating the differential of $\alpha$), while $\omega_1$ does not. We get a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
<!-- theorem-17: body_md -->
\label{mumford}
There exists a positive constants $c_3=c_3(g+t,d)>0$ satisfying the property as follows. Let $G$ be a principally polarized semiabelian variety over $\overline\mathbb{Q}$ of dimension $g+t$. 

Let $X\subset G$ be a closed subvariety of degree $d$ generating $A$. Assume $X$ has finite stabilizer. Then there exists a reduced subscheme $Z\subsetneq X$ of degree $${\mathrm{deg}} Z\le c_1(g+t,d),$$ and a point $g_0\in G(\overline{\mathbb Q})$ such that for any $g_1\in G(\overline{\mathbb Q})$, we have
$$\{x\in X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q}):\widehat{h}(x-g_1)\le c_3(g+t,d)\widehat h(g_1-g_0)\}\subset Z(\overline\mathbb{Q}).$$
<!-- end theorem-17 -->
<!-- proof-35: body_md -->
Let $c_0$ and $g_0$ be as in forthcoming Proposition \ref{prop_height_inequality_translation}.
Let $c_2$ be as in Theorem \ref{bogomolov}. Set $c_3=c_2/c_0.$ 
Then we conclude the proof by applying Theorem \ref{bogomolov} to $X+g_1\subset G$.
<!-- end proof-35 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lemma_maximal_stable_under_translation}
    Put $S^\circ:=\{s\in S\,:\, \mathfrak X_s \text{ has finite stabilier}\}$. Then $S^\circ$ is open in $S$ and stable under translation.
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-36: body_md -->
It suffices to prove that $S^\circ$ is open in $S$.
Let $m:{\mathcal G}\times_S{\mathcal G}\to{\mathcal G}$ be the multiplication map. Then ${\mathcal G}\times_S{\mathcal G}$ is a semiabelian scheme over ${\mathcal G}$, where the structure morphism is the second projection, and $m^{-1}{\mathcal X}\subset{\mathcal G}\times_S{\mathcal G}$ is faithfully flat over the base ${\mathcal G}$ with geometrically integral fibers. 

Consider the closed subset $Z=m^{-1}{\mathcal X}\cap p_1^{-1}{\mathcal X}\subset{\mathcal G}\times_S{\mathcal G}$. For any point $g_1\in{\mathcal G}(\overline\mathbb{Q})$, it is in the stabilizer of ${\mathcal X}_{\pi_{\mathcal G/S}(g_1)}$ if and only if $\dim(p_2^{-1}(g_1)\cap Z)$ equals the relative dimension $d$ of ${\mathcal X}$ over $S$. By the semi-continuity of fiber dimension, such points form a Zariski closed subset $Y\subset{\mathcal G}$, as the relative dimension of $Z$ over the second $\mathcal G$ is a most $d$. 
Then $$S^\circ=\{s\in S\,:\, \dim Y_s=0\}.$$
Notice that $Y$ maps to $S$ surjectively since the stabilizer always contains the identity. Then again by the semi-continuity of fiber dimension, $S^\circ$ is open in $S.$
<!-- end proof-36 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lemm_SUT_disjoint_union}
    Assume that $S_1\sqcup S_2\subset S$ is stable under translation. If $S_1$ is stable under translation, then so is $S_2.$
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-37: body_md -->
Assume that there exists $s_2\in S_2$ and $g_2\in \mathcal P_{\pi_{S/B}(s_2)}$ such that $g_2\cdot s_2\in S_1$. Then
    $s_2=(-g_2)\cdot (g_2\cdot s_1)$ which contradicts to the stability of $S_1$.
<!-- end proof-37 -->
<!-- proposition-14: body_md -->
\label{prop_height_inequality_translation}
There exists a positive constant $c_0=c_0(g+t,d)>0$ satisfying the property as follows. Let $G$ be a principally polarized semiabelian variety over $\overline\mathbb{Q}$ of dimension $g+t$. Let $X\subset G$ be a closed subvariety of degree $d$. Assume $X$ has finite stabilizer. Then there exists a point $g_0\in G(\overline\mathbb{Q})$ such that for any $g_1\in G(\overline\mathbb{Q})$,
$$h([X+g_1])\ge c_0\widehat{h}(g_1-g_0).$$
<!-- end proposition-14 -->
<!-- proof-38: body_md -->
After running $\chi$ over all possible Hilbert polynomials (which form a finite set),
it suffices to prove that for any irreducible subset $S_1\subset S^\circ$ stable under translation, there is a positive constant $c_0(S_1)>0$ such that the following holds:\begin{equation}\label{eq_translation_minimum}\begin{aligned}
    &\text{for any }s\in S_1(\overline\mathbb{Q})\text{, there is a point }g_s\in{\mathcal G}_s(\overline\mathbb{Q})\text{ satisfying }\\
&\kern5em h([{\mathcal X}_s+g_1])\ge c_0(S_1)\widehat{h}(g_1-g_s)\\
&\text{for any }g_1\in{\mathcal G}_s(\overline\mathbb{Q}).
\end{aligned} 
\end{equation}
Indeed, since $S^\circ$ itself is stable under invariant by Lemma \ref{lemma_maximal_stable_under_translation}, we only need to set $$c_0=\min\{c_0(S_1)\,:\, S_1 \text{ is a irreducible component of }S^\circ\}$$.
We prove by induction on $\dim S_1$. 
Fix a point $s_0\in S_1(\overline\mathbb{Q})$. Since $S_1\subset S^\circ$, the orbit $$\mathcal P_{\pi_{S/B}(s_0)}\cdot s_0=f(f^{-1}(s_0)),$$ which represents all translation of $\mathcal X_{s_0}$, is of dimension $g+t$.

Take a closed subvariety $W\subset S_1$ such that $\dim W=\dim S_1-(g+t)$ and $W$ intersects $f(f^{-1}(s_0))$ at finitely many points (not empty). Let $f_0:=f|_{{\mathcal G}_{W}}:{\mathcal G}_{W}\to S_1.$
Since $$\dim \mathcal G_W= \dim (\mathcal P\times_B W)=\dim W+g+t=\dim S_1,$$
and $f_0$ has finite fiber over $s_0$, by the semi-continuity of fiber dimension, $f_0$ is dominant and generically quasi-finite. 

Note that for $s\in S_1$ and $g_2\in \mathcal P_{\pi_{S/B}(s)},$
\begin{align*}
    f_0^{-1}(g_2\cdot s)&=\{(g_1,w)\,:\, g_1\cdot w=g_2\cdot s, w\in W_{\pi_{S/B}(s)},g_1\in \mathcal P_{\pi_{S/B}(s)}\}\\
    &=\{(g_2+g'_1,w')\,:\, (g_1',w')\in f_0^{-1}(s)\}.
\end{align*}
Therefore if we set
$$\begin{cases}
    S_0:=S_1\setminus f_0(\mathcal G_W),\\
    S_{\mathrm{fin}}:=\{s\in S_1\, :\, \dim f_0^{-1}(s)=0\},\\
    S_{\infty}:=\{s\in S_1\,:\, \dim f_0^{-1}(s)\geq 1\},
\end{cases}$$
then $S_0, S_{\mathrm{fin}}$ and $S_\infty$ is stable under translation. Moreover, $S_{\infty}\subsetneq S_1$ is Zariski closed.

Let $S'$ be the largest open subset of $S_{\mathrm{fin}}$ contained in $S_{\mathrm{fin}}\setminus S_0=f(\mathcal G_W)\setminus S_\infty=f(\mathcal G_{W}\setminus S_\infty)$. It is non-empty by Chevalley's theorem. 

We claim that $S_1\setminus S'$ is stable under translation. Hence by Lemma \ref{lemm_SUT_disjoint_union}, so is $S'$. Since $S_1\setminus S'=(S_{\mathrm{fin}}\setminus S')\sqcup S_{\infty}$, it suffices to show that $S_{\mathrm{fin}}\setminus S'$ is stable under translation.
Consider the set
\begin{align*}
    R&=\pi^{-1}_{\mathcal G/S}(S_{\mathrm{fin}}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\setminus f(\mathcal G_W(\overline {\mathbb{Q}})))\subset\mathcal G_{S_{\mathrm{fin}}\setminus S'}(\overline{\mathbb Q}).
\end{align*}
which is dense in $\mathcal G_{S_{\mathrm{fin}}\setminus S'}$ by the maximality of $S'$ and the fact that $\pi_{\mathcal G/S}$ is open.

We show that $$f(R)\subset S_{\mathrm{fin}}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})\setminus f(\mathcal G_W(\overline {\mathbb{Q}})) \subset S_{\mathrm{fin}}(\overline {\mathbb{Q}})\setminus S'(\overline {\mathbb{Q}}).$$ Assume the contrary, then there exists $s\in S_{\mathrm{fin}}(\overline {\mathbb{Q}})\setminus f(\mathcal G_W(\overline {\mathbb{Q}}))$ and $g_1\in \mathcal P_{\pi_{S/B}(s)}(\overline {\mathbb{Q}})$ such that $g_1\cdot s=g_2\cdot w$ for $(g_2,w)\in \mathcal G_W(\overline {\mathbb{Q}}).$ Therefore $s=(-g_1+g_2)\cdot w\in f(\mathcal G_W(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}))$ which is a contradiction. By the density of $R$, we obtain that $S_{\mathrm{fin}}\setminus S'$ is stable under translation. 


Applying the induction hypothesis to irreducible components of $S_1\setminus S'$, we obtain a constant $c_0(S_1\setminus S')>0$ such that \eqref{eq_translation_minimum} holds for $S_1\setminus S'$. 

Recall the adelic line bundle $\overline H$ on $S$ defining the modular height. 
Put $W'=W\cap S'$ and $f':=f_0|_{\mathcal G_{W'}}:\mathcal G_{W'}\rightarrow S'$ which is surjective and quasi-finite.

Therefore $f'^*\overline H$ is big and nef on every closed subvariety of ${\mathcal G}_{W'}$. By Lemma \ref{lemma_height_ineq_nef_and_big}, there exists $c_0(S')>0$ such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq_height_ineq_modular}h_{f'^*\overline H}(\cdot)\ge c_0(S')\widehat{h}(\cdot)\end{equation}
on ${\mathcal G}_{W'}(\overline\mathbb{Q})$.

For any $s\in S'(\overline\mathbb{Q})$, that $f'$ is surjective implies $s=g_0\cdot w$ for some $w\in W'_{\pi_{S/B}(s)}$ and $g_0\in \mathcal P_{\pi_{S/B}(s)}$. For any $g_1\in{\mathcal G}_{s}(\overline\mathbb{Q})={\mathcal G}_w(\overline \mathbb{Q})=\mathcal P_{\pi_{S/B}(s)}(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$, we have $$(-g_1)\cdot s=(g_0-g_1)\cdot w={f'(g_0-g_1,w)}.$$ The above inequality \eqref{eq_height_ineq_modular} reads
$$h([{\mathcal X}_s+g_1])\geq h_{\overline H}((-g_1)\cdot s)=h_{f'^*\overline H}(g_0-g_1,w)\ge c_0(S')\widehat{h}(g_1-g_0).$$
We then conclude the proof by setting $c_0(S)=\min\{c_0(S'),c_0(S_1\setminus S')\}.$
<!-- end proof-38 -->
<!-- theorem-18: body_md -->
\label{ML}
There exists a constant $c(g+t,d)$ satisfying the property as follows. Let $K$ be a field of characteristic $0$. Let $G$ be a polarized semiabelian variety over $K$ of dimension $g+t$. Let $\Gamma\subset G(K)$ be a subgroup of finite rank. Let $X\subset G$ be a closed subvariety of degree $d$. Then there are at most $c(g+t,d)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}$ cosets $H_1,H_2\dots$ contained in $X$ such that
$$X(K)\cap\Gamma=\bigcup H_i(K)\cap\Gamma.$$
<!-- end theorem-18 -->
<!-- proposition-15: body_md -->
\label{ML1}
There exists a constant $c_7(g+t,d,n)$ satisfying the property as follows. Let $G$ be a principally polarized semiabelian variety of dimension $g+t$ over $\overline\mathbb{Q}$. Let $X\subset G$ be a closed subvariety of degree $d$ and dimension $n$. Let $\Gamma\subset G(\overline\mathbb{Q})$ be a subgroup of finite rank. Then there exist reduced closed subschemes $Z_i\subsetneqq X$ $(i=1,2,\dots,c_7(g+t,d,n)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1})$ of degree at most $c_1(g+t,d)$ such that
$$\#(X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma)\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{c_7(g+t,d,n)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}}Z_i(\overline\mathbb{Q}).$$
Here $c_1(g+t,d)$ is the constant in Theorem \ref{bogomolov}
<!-- end proposition-15 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lemma_point_counting}
Let $P\subset\Gamma$ be a subset. Let $h_0,h_1>0$ be positive numbers. Assume that $\hat{h}(x)\le h_0$ for any $x_0\in P$, and $\hat{h}(x_1-x_2)\ge h_1$ for any distinct $x_1,x_2\in P$. Then
$$\# P\le\max\left\{\frac{4h_0}{h_1}+1,\sqrt\frac{8h_0}{h_1}+1\right\}^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}.$$
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-39: body_md -->
By the two assumptions, the union
$$\bigcup_{x\in P}B\left(x,\frac{1}{4}h_1,\sqrt{\frac{1}{8}h_1}\right)$$
is disjoint and contained in
$$B\left(0,h_0+\frac{1}{4}h_1,\sqrt{h_0}+\sqrt{\frac{1}{8}h_1}\right).$$
Computation of the volumes gives the conclusion.
<!-- end proof-39 -->
<!-- proof-40: body_md -->
Fix a level-$4$ structure on $G$. Take $g_0\in G(\overline\mathbb{Q})$ as in Theorem \ref{mumford}. We may assume $g_0=0$. Indeed, take $X'=X+g_0$ and the subgroup $\Gamma'\subset G(\overline\mathbb{Q})$ generated by $\Gamma$ and $g_0$. Then $\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)\le\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma')+1$. Once we have
$$\#((X')^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma')$$
is covered by $c_7(g+t,d,n)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma')+1}$ subschemes $Z_i$, this would implies
$$\#(X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma)\ \le\#(X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma')=\#((X')^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma')$$
is covered by
$$c_7(g+t,d,n)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma')+1}\le\max\{c_7(g+t,d,n)^2,1\}^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}$$
subschemes.

We list the results to be used in counting points.
\begin{enumerate}
    \item[(1)](Theorem \ref{bogomolov}) For any $x\in X(\overline\mathbb{Q})$, there exists a $Z_x\subset X$ of degree at most $c_1(g+t,d)$ such that
    $$\{y\in X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q}):\widehat h(y-x)\le c_2(g+t,d)h([X])\}\subset Z_x(\overline\mathbb{Q})$$
    \item[(2)](Theoerm \ref{mumford}) For any $x\in X(\overline\mathbb{Q})$, there exists a $Z_x'\subset X$ of degree at most $c_1(g+t,d)$ such that
    $$\{y\in X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q}):\widehat h(y-x)\le c_3(g+t,d)\widehat h(x)\}\subset Z_x'(\overline\mathbb{Q})$$
    \item[(3)](\cite[Theorem 4.1]{remond}) There exist positive constants $c_4(g+t,d,n),c_5(g+t,d,n)$ and $c_6(g+t,d,n)$ such that for $x_1,\dots,x_{n+1}\in X(\overline\mathbb{Q})$ satisfying
    $$h_{\overline M}\left(\frac{x_i}{\widehat{h}(x_i)}-\frac{x_{i+1}}{\widehat{h}(x_{i+1})}\right)\le\frac1{c_4},\quad h_{\overline L}\left(\frac{x_i}{\widehat{h}(x_i)}-\frac{x_{i+1}}{\widehat{h}(x_{i+1})}\right)\le\frac1{c_4^2},$$
    $$\widehat h(x_{i+1})\ge c_5^2\widehat h(x_i)\quad\mathrm{and}\quad\widehat{h}(x_1)\ge c_6h([X])\footnote{The original statement of \cite[Theorem 4.1]{remond} didn't provide uniform constants. However, in its proof, one can see that the constants are explicitly chosen using the notations appeared in \cite{remond2005ineq}, so that we get the inequality $\widehat h(x_1)\geq c_6'(g+t,d,n) \max \{h(X),(t+1)h_{\mathrm{add}}(A)\}$, where $h_{\mathrm{add}}(A)$ is a height function associated with the group law on the abelian quotient $A$. By \cite[(8.7)]{DGH}, $h_{\mathrm{add}}(A)\leq \ell \max\{1,h_{\mathrm{Fal}}(A)\}$, for some $\ell>0$, hence can be bounded by $h([X])$ up to a positive constant due to Lemma \ref{lemma_height_ineq_nef_and_big}. Combining with \eqref{eq_height_ineq_modular}, we obtain the current form.},$$
    we have $x_i\notin X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})$ for some $i$.
\end{enumerate}

In the following, we say $$\{x\in X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q}):\widehat{h}(x)\le c_6(g+t,d,n)h([X])\}$$
is the set of \emph{small points}. Its complement in $X^\circ(\overline {\mathbb{Q}})\cap\Gamma$ is called the set of \emph{large points}.

We take a maximal subset $P_1$ of the small points set
such that any distinct $x_1,x_2\in P_1$ satisfy
$$\widehat{h}(x_1-x_2)>c_2(g+t,d)h([X]).$$
By (1), small points are covered by
$$\bigcup_{x\in P_1}Z_x(\overline\mathbb{Q}).$$
By Lemma \ref{lemma_point_counting},
$$\#P_1\le\max\left\{\frac{4c_6(g+t,d,n)}{c_2(g+t,d)}+1,\sqrt\frac{8c_6(g+t,d,n)}{c_2(g+t,d)}+1\right\}^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}.$$
Denote the base number by $c_7'(g+t,d,n)$

For any $r>0$ and ratio $\kappa>1$, consider the annular region
$$A(r,\kappa)=\{x\in\Gamma\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb{R}:r\le\widehat{h}(x)\le\kappa r\}.$$
Choose a maximal subset $Q(r,\kappa)$ of $A(r,\kappa)$ such that any distinct $x_1,x_2\in Q(r,\kappa)$ satisfy
$$\widehat{h}(x_1-x_2)>c_3(g+t,d)r.$$
By (2), $X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap A(r,\kappa)$ is covered by
$$\bigcup_{x\in Q(r,\kappa)}Z_x'.$$
By Lemma \ref{lemma_point_counting},
$$\#Q(r,\kappa)\le\max\Big\{\frac{4\kappa}{c_3(g+t,d)}+1,\sqrt\frac{8\kappa}{c_2(g+t,d)}+1\Big\}^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}.$$
We take $\kappa=c_5^4(g+t,d,n)$. Then the base number of the right hand side depends only of $g+t,d$ and $n$. Denote it by $c_7''(g+t,d,n).$

Take a maximal subset $P_2$ of large points such that any distinct $x_1,x_2\in P_2$ satisfy either
$${h}_{\overline M}\left(\frac{x_1}{\widehat h(x_1)}-\frac{x_2}{\widehat h(x_2)}\right)>\frac1{c_4(g+t,d,n)}$$
or
$${h}_{\overline L}\left(\frac{x_1}{\widehat h(x_1)}-\frac{x_2}{\widehat h(x_2)}\right)>\frac1{c_4^2(g+t,d,n)}.$$
Then large points is covered by the cones
$$\left\{y\in\Gamma\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\mathbb{R}:{h}_{\overline M}\left(\frac{y}{\widehat h(y)}-\frac{x}{\widehat h(x)}\right)\le\frac1{c_4(g+t,d,n)},{h}_{\overline L}\left(\frac{y}{\widehat h(y)}-\frac{x}{\widehat h(x)}\right)\le\frac1{c_4^2(g+t,d,n)}\right\}$$
for $x\in P_2$. By (3), every cone is covered by $n$ annuli. Now it remains to bound $\# P_2$. Since
$$\bigcup_{x\in P_2}B\left(\frac x{\widehat h(x)},\frac{1}{2c_4(g+t,d,n)},\frac{1}{2c_4(g+t,d,n)}\right)$$
is a disjoint union contained in $\displaystyle B\left(0,1+\frac{1}{2c_4(g+t,d,n)},1+\frac{1}{2c_4(g+t,d,n)}\right)$, we get
$$\#P_2\le(2c_4(g+t,d,n)+1)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}.$$

In conclusion, the number of reduced subschemes $Z$ of degree at most $c_1$ that we need to cover $X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma$ is
$$(c_7')^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}+n(c_7'')^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}(2c_4+1)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}\le\Big(c_7'+nc_7''(2c_4+1)\Big)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}.$$
<!-- end proof-40 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{pp_reduction_lemma}
There exists a constant $a(g+t,d)$ satisfying the property as follows. For any polarized semiabelian variety $(G,L)$ of dimension $g+t$ and subvariety $X$ of degree $d$, if $X$ generates the abelian quotient $A$, then there exists a principally polarized semiabelian variety $(G',L')$ and an isogeny $f:G'\to G$ of degree at most $a(g+t,d)$ such that $f^*L$ is proportional to $L'$, i.e., $f^*L\cong nL'$ for some $n\ge1$. Moreover, the restriction of $f$ on the toric part is the identity.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-41: body_md -->
Denote $Y={\pi(\overline X)}\subset A$.
By \cite[Lemma 2.2 \& Lemma 2.5]{GGK}, there is an isogeny $f'_{\mathrm{ab}}:A\to A'$ such that ${\mathrm{deg}}(f'_{\mathrm{ab}})\le a'(g+t,{\mathrm{deg}}_L(Y))$ for some constant $a'$ and a principal polarization $L'$ on $A'$ such that $(f'_{\mathrm{ab}})^*L'\cong L$. Since $L$ and $M$ are nef, we have $${\mathrm{deg}}_L(Y)=(L|_{Y}^{\dim Y})\le(\pi^*L|_{\overline X}^{\dim Y})\cdot(M|_{\overline X}^{\dim X-\dim Y})\le(L+M)|_{\overline X}^{\dim X}=d$$
where the first inequality is due to the projection formula, and the second is due to the binomial expansion. We may assume that $a$ is increasing in ${\mathrm{deg}}_L(Y)$, then $${\mathrm{deg}}(f_{\mathrm{ab}}')\leq a'(g+t,d).$$ 
Take a quasi-inverse $f_{\mathrm{ab}}:A'\to A$ of $f_{\mathrm{ab}}'$, i.e., $f_{\mathrm{ab}}$ is an isogeny such that $f_{\mathrm{ab}}'\circ f_{\mathrm{ab}}=[{\mathrm{deg}}(f'_{\mathrm{ab}})]:A'\to A'$. Then ${\mathrm{deg}}(f_{\mathrm{ab}})\le{\mathrm{deg}}(f'_{\mathrm{ab}})^{g+t}\le a'(g+t,d)^{g+t}$ and
$$f_{\mathrm{ab}}^*L=f^*_{\mathrm{ab}}(f'_{\mathrm{ab}})^*L'={\mathrm{deg}}(f'_{\mathrm{ab}})^2L'.$$
We then set $G'$ to be the pull-back of $G$ via $f_{\mathrm{ab}}$, and $a(g+t,d):=a'(g+t,d)^{g+t}$. Then $G',L'$ and $a$ are as desired.
<!-- end proof-41 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{MLforpoints}
There exists a constant $c'(g+t,d)$ satisfying the property as follows. Let $G$ be a polarized semiabelian variety of dimension $g+t$ over $\overline\mathbb{Q}$. Let $X\subset G$ be a reduced closed subscheme of degree $d$. Let $\Gamma\subset G(\overline\mathbb{Q})$ be a subgroup of finite rank. Then
$$\#(X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma)\le c'(g+t,d)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}.$$
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-42: body_md -->
We proceed by induction on $\dim X.$

If $\dim X=0$, then
$$\#(X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma)\le\# X(\overline\mathbb{Q})=d.$$
Assume that proposition statement holds in the case that $\dim X<n$ with constant $c^*(g+t,d,n).$

We now prove it in the case that \begin{equation*}
   \kern-4em\text{(HP0)}\qquad \dim X=n.
\end{equation*}

{\textbf{Step 1.}} First, we reduce to the case that
\begin{equation*}
     \text{(HP1)}\quad
        X\text{ is irreducible, and generates }A. 
\end{equation*}
Assume that the statement of the proposition holds under (HP0-1) for some constant $c''(g+t,d,n).$ We may and do further assume that $c''(g+t,d,n)\geq c^*(g+t,d,n)$ after replacing $c''$ with $\max\{c'',c^*\}.$ Moreover we assume that $c''(g+t,d,n)$ is increasing in $g+t$ and $d$ by replacing $c''(g+t,d,n)$ with
$$\max_{0\le i\le g+t,1\le j\le d}c''(i,j,n).$$

Let $X_1,X_2,\dots, X_m(m\leq d)$ be irreducible components of $X.$ 
For each $i=1,\dots,m$, put $A_i$ to be the abelian subvariety of $A$ generated by $X_i$, and take any $x_i\in X_i(\overline{\mathbb{Q}})$ such that $\pi(X_i-x_i)\subset A_i.$ We set $G_i=\pi^{-1}(A_i)$ and $\Gamma_i:=\langle x_i,\Gamma\rangle\cap G_i(\overline \mathbb{Q}).$ Hence $\mathrm{rk} \Gamma_i\leq \mathrm{rk} \Gamma+1.$

Then
\begin{align*}
\#(X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma)&\ \le\sum_{i=1}^m\#(X_i^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma)\\
&\ \le\sum\# ((X_i-x_i)^\circ (\overline \mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma_i)\\
&\ \le\sum_{i=1}^mc''(\dim A_i+t,{\mathrm{deg}} X_i,n)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma_i)+1}\\
&\ \le\Big(dc''(g+t,d,n)\Big)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+2},\\
&\ \leq c'^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}
\end{align*}
where
$$c':=(dc''(g+t,d,n))^2$$
depends only on $g+t,d$ and $n$.

\textbf{Step 2.} Under the assumption (HP1), now we further reduce to the case that
\begin{equation*}
    \text{(HP2)}\quad G\text{ is principally polarized.} 
\end{equation*}
Assume that the proposition holds under hypothesis (HP0-2) for some constant $c'''(g+t,d,n)$. We want to show that the proposition holds under only (HP0-1). Again, we may assume that $c'''(g+t,d,n)\geq c^*(g+t,d,n).$

By Lemma \ref{pp_reduction_lemma}, there is an isogeny $f:G'\to G$ of degree at most $a(g+t,d)$ such that $f^*L$ is proportional to a principal polarization $L'$ on $G'$. Take an irreducible component $X'$ of $f^{-1}(X)$ which maps onto $X$, which exists because $f:f^{-1}(X)\to X$ is étale and finite.

Note that $f$ is the identity if restricted to the toric part. Therefore we we have the extension $\overline f:\overline G'\rightarrow \overline G$ which is finite of the same degree as $f$. If we denote that $M':=\mathcal{O}_{\overline G'}(\overline G'\setminus G')$, then we have $M'=\overline f^*M.$ We have
\begin{align*}{\mathrm{deg}}_{L'+M'}(\overline {X'})&\le {\mathrm{deg}}_{\overline f^*L+M'}(\overline {X'})={\mathrm{deg}}_{\overline f^*(L+M)}(\overline {X'})\\&={\mathrm{deg}}(f){\mathrm{deg}}_{L+M}(\overline X)\le a(g+t,d)d\end{align*}
where the first inequality is due the nefness of $L'$ and $M'$.

We may assume that $c'''(g+t,d,n)$ is increasing in $d$. Then
$$\#((X')^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap f^{-1}(\Gamma))\le c'''(g+t,a(g+t,d)d,n)^{\mathrm{rk}(f^{-1}(\Gamma))+1}.$$
Since $f$ is an isogeny, $f^{-1}(\Gamma)\to\Gamma$ is surjective with finite kernel, and hence $\mathrm{rk}(f^{-1}(\Gamma))=\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)$.

For any $x\in X^{\circ}(\overline \mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma$, there is an $x'\in X'(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap f^{-1}(\Gamma)$ such that $f(x')=x$. Moreover, we have $x'\in (X')^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})$. Otherwise $x'\in H'(\overline\mathbb{Q})$ for some positive dimensional coset $H'\subset X'$. Then $x\in f(H')(\overline\mathbb{Q})$, where $f(H')\subset X$ is a positive dimension coset, contradicting $x\in X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})$. Therefore,
$$\#(X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma)\le\#((X')^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap f^{-1}(\Gamma))\le c'''(g+t,a(g+t,d)d,n)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}.$$
We thus set $c''(g+t,d,n)=c'''(g+t,a(g+t,d)d,n).$

\textbf{Step 3.} Now  it suffices to prove the proposition under the assumption (HP0-2).
Applying Proposition \ref{ML1} to $X$, we get reduced closed subschemes $Z_i\subset X$ $(i=1,2,\dots,c_7(g+t,d,n)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1})$ of degree at most $c_1(g+t,d)$. By the induction hypthesis,
$$\#(Z_i^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma)\le c^*(g+t,c_1(g+t,d),n)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}.$$
Since $X^\circ\cap Z_i\subset Z_i^\circ$,
$$\#(X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma)\le(c_7(g+t,d,n)c^*(g+t,c_1(g+t,d),n))^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}.$$
<!-- end proof-42 -->
<!-- head-2: body_md -->
First, we reduce to the case that
\begin{equation*}
     \text{(HP1)}\quad
        X\text{ is irreducible, and generates }A. 
\end{equation*}
Assume that the statement of the proposition holds under (HP0-1) for some constant $c''(g+t,d,n).$ We may and do further assume that $c''(g+t,d,n)\geq c^*(g+t,d,n)$ after replacing $c''$ with $\max\{c'',c^*\}.$ Moreover we assume that $c''(g+t,d,n)$ is increasing in $g+t$ and $d$ by replacing $c''(g+t,d,n)$ with
$$\max_{0\le i\le g+t,1\le j\le d}c''(i,j,n).$$
<!-- end head-2 -->
<!-- head-3: body_md -->
Under the assumption (HP1), now we further reduce to the case that
\begin{equation*}
    \text{(HP2)}\quad G\text{ is principally polarized.} 
\end{equation*}
Assume that the proposition holds under hypothesis (HP0-2) for some constant $c'''(g+t,d,n)$. We want to show that the proposition holds under only (HP0-1). Again, we may assume that $c'''(g+t,d,n)\geq c^*(g+t,d,n).$
<!-- end head-3 -->
<!-- head-4: body_md -->
Now  it suffices to prove the proposition under the assumption (HP0-2).
Applying Proposition \ref{ML1} to $X$, we get reduced closed subschemes $Z_i\subset X$ $(i=1,2,\dots,c_7(g+t,d,n)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1})$ of degree at most $c_1(g+t,d)$. By the induction hypthesis,
$$\#(Z_i^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma)\le c^*(g+t,c_1(g+t,d),n)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}.$$
Since $X^\circ\cap Z_i\subset Z_i^\circ$,
$$\#(X^\circ(\overline\mathbb{Q})\cap\Gamma)\le(c_7(g+t,d,n)c^*(g+t,c_1(g+t,d),n))^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}.$$
<!-- end head-4 -->
<!-- proposition-16: body_md -->
\label{prop_relative_ueno} 
There are finitely many pairs $(S_1,{\mathcal G}_1),(S_2,{\mathcal G}_2)\dots(S_N,{\mathcal G}_N)$ of a closed subvariety $S_i\subset S$ and a semiabelian subscheme ${\mathcal G}_i\subset{\mathcal G}_{S_i}={\mathcal G}\times_SS_i$ such that for any $s\in S(K)$, the Ueno locus of ${\mathcal X}_s$ is a union of cosets of ${\mathcal G}_{i,s}$ for $S_i$ containing $s$.

In particular, the relative Ueno locus is a Zariski closed set.
<!-- end proposition-16 -->
<!-- lemma-15: body_md -->
\label{lemma_fiber_weakly_special_subvariety}
Let $M\subset\mathcal P_{g,t}^\times$ be a special subvariety with connected Mixed Shimura datum $(Q,\mathcal Y^+)$. Let $N\trianglelefteq Q$ be a normal subgroup. Denote $S=\pi_{\mathrm{sab}}(M)\subset(\mathcal A_g^\vee)^{[t]}$ and $\mathcal G=\pi_{\mathrm{sab}}^{-1}(S)$. Then there is a semiabelian subscheme $\mathcal H\subset\mathcal G$ such that for any $\widetilde y\in\mathcal Y^+$ and $s\in S(\mathbb{C})$, each irreducible component of $\mathbf{u}(N(\mathbb R)^+U_N(\mathbb C)\widetilde y)\cap \pi_{\mathrm{sab}}^{-1}(s)$ is a coset of $\mathcal H_s$.
<!-- end lemma-15 -->
<!-- proof-43: body_md -->
It can be verified that $\mathcal G$ is also a special subvariety with the connected mixed Shimura datum $(Q_1,\mathcal Y_1^+)$ for
$$Q_1=(\mathrm M_{t,1}\oplus \mathrm M_{2g,1})\cdot Q,\quad\mathcal Y_1^+=\mathrm M_{t,1}(\mathbb{C})\times \mathrm M_{2g,1}(\mathbb{R})\times\widetilde{\pi}_{\mathrm{sab}}(\mathcal Y^+).$$

Since $\mathrm M_{t,1}\oplus \mathrm M_{2g,1}$ is normal in $P_{g,t}$, $(U_N\oplus V_N)=(\mathrm M_{t,1}\oplus \mathrm M_{2g,1})\cap N$ is normal in $Q_1$.

By the same argument as in the proof of Corollary \ref{coro_semiabelian_subscheme}, we have a semiabelian subcheme $\mathcal H$ of $\mathcal G$ such that the Shimura quotient $\mathcal G_{/(U_N\oplus V_N)}$ is the quotient $\mathcal G/\mathcal H$ as semiabelian scheme over $S$.

Note that $$\rho_{/(U_N\oplus V_N)}(\mathbf{u}(N(\mathbb{R})^+ U_N(\mathbb{C})\widetilde y))=\mathbf{u}(p_{\mathrm{sab}}(N)(\mathbb{R})^+\widetilde\pi_{\mathrm{sab}}(\widetilde y))\subset \mathcal G/\mathcal H$$ is a multi-section of $S$, and $\mathbf{u}(N(\mathbb{R})^+U_N(\mathbb{C})\widetilde y)\cap \pi_{\mathrm{sab}}^{-1}(s)$ is exactly the preimage of $\pi_{\mathrm{sab}}^{-1}(s)\cap \mathbf{u}(p_{\mathrm{sab}}(N)(\mathbb{R})^+\widetilde\pi_{\mathrm{sab}}(\widetilde y))$, which concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-43 -->
<!-- proof-44: body_md -->
To see how the first assertion implies the Ueno locus is Zariski closed, consider the quotient map $f_i:{\mathcal G}_{S_i}\to{\mathcal G}_{S_i}/{\mathcal G}_i$. Then the set
$$\{z\in \mathcal G_{S_i}\,:\, \dim_z (f_i^{-1}(f_i(z))\cap \mathcal X)\geq \dim \mathcal G_i-\dim S_i\}$$
is Zariski closed by the upper semicontinuity, and the relative Ueno locus is the union of all such set.

Now we prove the first assertion, i.e., the finiteness result.
We may assume ${\mathcal G}/S$ is principally polarized with a level-$4$ structure by taking a finite étale cover. So there exist modular maps $\mathcal G\to\mathcal P_{g,t}^\times$ and $S\rightarrow (\mathcal A_g^\vee)^{[t]} $. After taking an embedding $K\hookrightarrow \mathbb{C}$, we may also assume $K=\mathbb{C}$. Note that there is no loss of generality since if a semiabelian variety $G$ is defined over $K$, then any semiabelian subvariety $G'\subset G_\mathbb{C}$ is defined over $K$ (see for example the proof of \cite[Proposition 3.7]{Yamaki2018trace} or \cite[Theorem B]{liu2024chowtrace1motiveslangneron}).

We first assume that the modular map is injective. Recall the geometric Zilber--Pink \cite[Theorem 7.1]{BU}. The case $\delta_{\mathrm{ws}}=0$ states that there are finitely many triplets $(Q_i,\mathcal Y_i^+,N_i)$, where $(Q_i,\mathcal Y_i^+)$ is a connected mixed Shimura subdatum and $N_i\trianglelefteq Q_i$ is a normal subgroup with reductive part being semisimple, such that each weakly optimal and weakly special subset of ${\mathcal X}$ is of form $\mathbf{u}(U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})N_i(\mathbb{R})^+\widetilde y_i)$ for some $\widetilde y_i\in \mathcal Y_i^+$.

Fix an index $i$. We show that for any $\widetilde y\in\mathcal{Y}_i^+$ and $s\in S(K)$, each irreducible component of $\mathbf{u}(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\widetilde y)\cap{\mathcal G}_s$ is of dimension $$\dim(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\cap (\mathrm M_{t,1}(\mathbb{C})\oplus \mathrm M_{2g,1}(\mathbb{R})),$$ which depends only on $i$. Note that it is not necessarily non-empty. For any
$$y'\in \mathbf{u}(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\widetilde y)\cap{\mathcal G}_s,$$
there is a lifting $\widetilde y'$ such that
$$\mathbf{u}(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\widetilde y)=\mathbf{u}(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\widetilde y')$$
and
$${\mathcal G}_s=\mathbf{u}((\mathrm M_{t,1}(\mathbb{C})\oplus \mathrm M_{2g,1}(\mathbb{R}))\widetilde y').$$
Since $\mathbf{u}$ is a local diffeomorphism, we obtain that that $\mathbf{u}(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\widetilde y)\cap{\mathcal G}_s$ is of the same dimension as
$$(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\widetilde y')\cap (\mathrm M_{t,1}(\mathbb{C})\oplus \mathrm M_{2g,1}(\mathbb{R}))\widetilde y')$$
near $\widetilde y'$, which is exactly $\dim(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\cap (\mathrm M_{t,1}(\mathbb{C})\oplus \mathrm M_{2g,1}(\mathbb{R}))$.

Let $I$ be the set of index satisfying that 
$$\dim(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\cap (\mathrm M_{t,1}(\mathbb{C})\oplus \mathrm M_{2g,1}(\mathbb{R})))>0.$$
We claim any maximal coset $Z$ of positive dimension in ${\mathcal X}_s$ is an irreducible component of $\mathbf{u}(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\widetilde y)\cap{\mathcal G}_s$ for some $i\in I$. Indeed, since $Z$ is weakly special by \cite[Proposition 7.2]{ZGAxLindemann}, $Z$ is contained in some weakly optimal weakly special subset $\mathbf{u}(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\widetilde y)\subset{\mathcal X}$. Therefore $\mathbf{u}(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\widetilde y)\cap{\mathcal G}_s\subset \mathcal X_s$, whose irreducible components are cosets.  We thus obtain the claim by the maximality of $Z$.

For any $i\in I$, by Lemma \ref{lemma_fiber_weakly_special_subvariety}, for $S_i=\pi_{\mathrm{sab}}(\mathbf{u}(\mathcal Y_i^+))\cap S$, there is a subgroup scheme $\mathcal G_i\subset\mathcal G_{S_i}$ such that each irreducible component of $\mathbf{u}(N_i(\mathbb{R})^+ U_{N_i}(\mathbb{C})\widetilde y)\cap\mathcal G_s$ is a coset of $(\mathcal G_i)_s$ for $s\in S_i(K)$. This concludes the proof under the assumption that the modular map is injective.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        

In general, we use a self-product argument to reduce to the previous case.

Take an integer $n$ strictly larger than the dimension of any fiber of $S\to(\mathcal{A}_g^\vee)^{[t]}$. Let ${\mathcal Y}$ be the image of $$\mathcal X^{[n]}\rightarrow (\mathcal P_{g,t}^\times)^{[n]}\hookrightarrow\mathcal P_{ng,nt}^\times.$$ Denote by $\iota:S\to(\mathcal A_{ng}^\vee)^{[nt]}$ the moduli map. Note that the dimension of any fiber of $\iota$ is still strictly smaller than $n$. We prove that for any $s\in S(K)$ and subgroup variety $H\subset{\mathcal G}_s$, there is a coset of $H^n$ contained in ${\mathcal Y}_{\iota(s)}$ if and only if there is a coset of $H$ contained in ${\mathcal X}_{s'}$ for some $s'\in\iota^{-1}(\iota(s))$. Note that $\iota(s')=\iota(s)$ implies ${\mathcal G}_{s'}={\mathcal G}_s$ since $(\mathcal A_{ng}^\vee)^{[nt]}$ is a fine moduli space. Hence we can view $H$ as a subgroup of ${\mathcal G}_{s'}$.

The ``if" part is obvious since $({\mathcal X}_{s'})^n\subset{\mathcal Y}_{\iota(s)}$ for any $s\in S(K)$. Conversely, assume $H$ satisfies that $H^n+(x_1,\dots,x_n)\subset{\mathcal Y}_{\iota(s)}$ for $x_1,\dots,x_n\in{\mathcal X}_s$. Let $W$ be its preimage in $\mathcal X^{[n]}$. Then $\dim W\ge n\dim H.$

Note that $W$ lies over $\iota^{-1}(\iota(s))\subset S$. Denote by $D(W,\iota^{-1}(\iota(s)))$ the maximal dimension of fiber of $W$ over $\iota^{-1}(\iota(s))$. The notation applies to other schemes. Then
$$D(W,\iota^{-1}(\iota(s)))\le\sum_{i=1}^n D(p_i(W),\iota^{-1}(\iota(s))),$$
where $p_i:\mathcal X^{[n]}\to{\mathcal X}$ is the $i$-th projection. By our choice, $n>\dim(\iota^{-1}(\iota(s)))$. So 
$$D(W,\iota^{-1}(\iota(s)))\ge\dim W-\dim(\iota^{-1}(\iota(s)))>n(\dim H-1).$$
By the pigeonhole principle,
$$D(p_i(W),\iota^{-1}(\iota(s)))\ge\dim H$$
for some $i$. However, $p_i(W)\subset{\mathcal G}_{\iota^{-1}(\iota(s))}={\mathcal G}_s\times\iota^{-1}(\iota(s))$ satisfies $p_i(W)\subset (H+x_i)\times\iota^{-1}(\iota(s))$. So for any $s'\in\iota^{-1}(\iota(s))$ satisfying that $\dim p_i(W)_{s'}=\dim H$, we have $(H+x_i)\subset\mathcal X_{s'}$.

By the previous case, there exist closed subvarieties $S'_\ell\subset \iota(S)$ and semiabelian subschemes $\mathcal H'_\ell\subset \mathcal G'_{S'_\ell}$ such that the proposition statement holds for $\mathcal Y$, where $\mathcal G'$ is the image of $\mathcal G^{[n]}$ in $\mathcal P^\times_{ng,nt}$. 

Let $\{S_i\}$ be the set $\{\text{irreducible components of }\iota^{-1}(S_\ell')\}$.
In the following, we take the convention of index that $S_i$ is an irreducible component of $\iota^{-1}(S_\ell').$ Let $\mathcal H_i=(\mathcal H_{\ell}')\times_{S_\ell'}S_i\subset (\mathcal G^{[n]})_{S_i}.$
Denote by $s_j:{\mathcal G}\to{\mathcal G}^{[n]}$ the $j$-th coordinate. 
Then we put 
$${\mathcal G}_i=\text{the neutral component of }\bigcap_{j=1}^ns_j^*{\mathcal H}_i,$$
which makes the proposition statement hold for ${\mathcal X}$ (here the equality means ${\mathcal G}_i$ is the largest semiabelian subscheme such that ${\mathcal G}_i^n\subset{\mathcal H}_i$).
<!-- end proof-44 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
Let ${\mathcal X}/S$ be as above. For each geometric point $\bar\eta$ of $S$, the Ueno locus of ${\mathcal X}_{\bar\eta}$ is the pull-back of the relative Ueno locus along $\bar\eta$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-45: body_md -->
Let $Y$ be the Ueno locus of ${\mathcal X}_{\bar\eta}$ and ${\mathcal Z}$ be the relative Ueno locus. For the Zariski closure ${\mathcal Y}$ of $Y$ in ${\mathcal X}$ and each point $s\in S(K)$, ${\mathcal Y}_s$ is a union of positive dimensional cosets and hence ${\mathcal Y}_s\subset{\mathcal Z}_s$. So ${\mathcal Y}\subset{\mathcal Z}$ and $Y\subset{\mathcal Z}_{\bar\eta}$. Conversely, by the above proposition, ${\mathcal Z}_{\bar\eta}$ is a union of positive dimensional cosets. Therefore, ${\mathcal Z}_{\bar\eta}\subset Y$.
<!-- end proof-45 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{coro_MLforpointsgeneralpol}
Let $c'(g+t,d)$ be as in Corollary \ref{MLforpoints}. Let $G$ be a polarized semiabelian variety of dimension $g+t$ over an algebraically closed field $K$ of characteristic $0$. Let $X\subset G$ be a reduced closed subscheme of degree $d$. Let $\Gamma\subset G(K)$ be a subgroup of finite rank. Then
$$\#(X^\circ(K)\cap\Gamma)\le c'(g+t,d)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}.$$
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-46: body_md -->
We first reduces to the case that $\Gamma$ is finitely generated. Assume that corollary statement holds for any finitely generated group. For a $\Gamma\subset G(K)$ of finite rank, we first take $\Gamma_1$ to be a finitely generated subgroup of $\Gamma$ which is of the same rank as $\Gamma$. For $i\geq 2$, let $$\Gamma_{i}:=\Gamma_1\cap\{x\in\Gamma \text{ is a torsion element of order at most } i\}.$$ Then $\Gamma_1\subset\Gamma_2\subset \Gamma_3\subset\cdots$, and $\Gamma=\cup\Gamma_i.$
Therefore we obtain that $\#X^\circ (K)\cap \Gamma\leq c'(g+t,d)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}$ as $\#X^\circ (K)\cap \Gamma_i\leq c'(g+t,d)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}$.

From now on, we assume that $\Gamma$ is finitely generated.
Take a subfield $F\subset K$ finitely generated over $\overline Q$, over which $G,\Gamma,X$ and the Ueno locus of $X$ are defined. We may assume $F=\overline \mathbb{Q}(S)$ for some quasi-projective variety $S$ over $\overline \mathbb{Q}$, hence $F\hookrightarrow K$ induces the geometric generic point $\overline \eta$ of $S$. 

By shrinking $S$, there is a semiabelian scheme ${\mathcal G}$ over $S$ and a closed subscheme ${\mathcal X}\subset{\mathcal G}$ faithfully flat over $S$ with geometrically integral fibers such that the geometric generic fiber is $X\subset G$.

Assume the contrary that
$$\#(X^\circ(K)\cap\Gamma)\ge c'(g+t,d)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}+1.$$
Fix $x_1,\dots,x_N\in X^\circ(K)\cap\Gamma$ for $N=c'(g+t,d)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}+1$. Again by shrinking $S$, we may assume that each $x_i$ extends to a section $\bar x_i:U\to{\mathcal X}_U$ such that for any $s\in S(\overline\mathbb{Q})$, $\bar x_i(s)$ are distinct and $\bar x_i(s)\in{\mathcal X}_s^\circ$, since the relative Ueno locus is Zariski closed. However, since the group generated by $\bar x_i(s)$ has rank at most $r$, this contradicts to Corollary \ref{MLforpoints}..
<!-- end proof-46 -->
<!-- proof-47: body_md -->
Without loss of generality, we assume that $K$ is algebraically closed. 

We proceed by induction on $g+t$. If $g+t=0$, there is nothing to prove. Assume that the theorem holds for semiabelian varieties of dimension smaller than $g+t.$

Now we want to prove that it holds for semiabelian varieties of dimension $g+t.$
We first reduces to the principally polarized case.
Assuming that Theorem \ref{ML} holds for principally polarized semiabelian varieties of dimension $g+t$, with the constant $c^\#(g+t,d).$

By Lemma \ref{pp_reduction_lemma}, there is an isogeny $f:G'\to G$ of degree at most $a(g+t,d)$ such that $f^*L$ is proportional to a principal polarization $L'$ on $G'$. Take an irreducible component $X'$ of $f^{-1}(X)$ which maps onto $X$. As in Step 2 of the proof to Corollary \ref{MLforpoints}, ${\mathrm{deg}}_{L'+M'}(\overline{X'})\le a(g+t,d)d$. So there are at most $c^\#(g+t,a(g+t,d)d)^{\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma)+1}$ cosets $H_1',H_2',\dots$ contained in $X'$ such that
$$X'(K)\cap f^{-1}(\Gamma)=\bigcup H_i'(K)\cap f^{-1}(\Gamma).$$
Here we used the fact that $\mathrm{rk}(f^{-1}(\Gamma))=\mathrm{rk}(\Gamma).$

Take $H_i=f(H_i)$. They are all cosets contained in $X$. For any point $x\in X(K)\cap\Gamma$, take a lifting $x'\in X'(K)\cap f^{-1}(\Gamma)$. Then $x'\in H_i'(K)$ for some $i$ and hence $x=f(x')\in H_i(K)$. Therefore,
$$X(K)\cap \Gamma\subset\bigcup H_i(K)\cap (\Gamma).$$

Now it suffices to prove the principally polarized case, which can be obtained from the following Lemma \ref{lemma_reduction_ML} and the induction hypothesis.
<!-- end proof-47 -->
<!-- lemma-16: body_md -->
\label{lemma_reduction_ML}
For any positive integers $g+t,d$, there exist an $N$ and a finite sequence of positive integers $d_1,\dots,d_N$ satisfying the property as follows. Let $G$ be a principally polarized semiabelian variety of dimension $g+t$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$. Let $X\subset G$ be a closed subvariety of degree $d$. Then there exists a subset $I_X\subset\{1,2,\dots N\}$, non-isogenous quotient maps $p_i:G\to G_i$ to polarized semiabelian subvarieties and closed subvarieties $X_i\subset G_i$ of degree at most $d_i$ for each $i\in I_X$ such that the Ueno locus of $X$ is the union of $f_i^{-1}(X_i)$.
<!-- end lemma-16 -->
<!-- proof-48: body_md -->
Apply Proposition \ref{prop_relative_ueno} to each irreducible component of the universal restricted Hilbert scheme. We use the same notation as in the proof of the second assertion of Proposition \ref{prop_relative_ueno}. Fix a polarization on each ${\mathcal G}_{S_i}/{\mathcal G}_i$ over $S_i$. Take the index set $I_X$ consisting of those $i$ such that $S_i$ contains the point representing $X$. For such $i$, let $p_i$ be the restriction of $f_i$ and $d_i$ be the maximal degree of fibers of ${\mathcal Z}_i$ over $S_i$. The existence of $d_i$ follows from generic flatness and induction on dimension.
<!-- end proof-48 -->
<!-- proposition-17: body_md -->
\label{prop_isogeny_trick} Let $G$ be a semiabelian variety, and $B\subset G^m$ be a semiabelian subvariety. We denote by $p_i$ the $i$-th projection $G^m\rightarrow G.$
Assume one of the following:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $G=\mathbb G_m^t$, $B$ is a subtorus;
    \item $B$ is an abelian subvariety.
\end{itemize}
Then there exists an isogeny $h:G^m\rightarrow G^m$ such that after reordering $G^m$, we have
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $h(B)=B_1\times \cdots\times B_m$ where $B_i=p_{i}(h(B));$
        \item $B_i\not=0$ if and only if $i\leq m'$ for some $0\leq m'\leq m;$
        \item For each $i=0,\dots, m-1$, $h$ preserves the subgroup $\mathrm{ker}(p_{1},\dots,p_i)$. If we denote the induced isogeny on $\mathrm{ker}(p_{1},\dots,p_i)\simeq G^{m-i}$ as $h^{(i)},$ then $h^{(m')}$ is the multiplication by $n$ map for some $n>0;$
        \item For each $i=1,\dots, m$ there exists an isogeny $h_i:G\rightarrow G$ such that 
        $$h_i\circ p_{i}= p_{i}\circ h^{(i-1)}.$$
    \end{enumerate}
<!-- end proposition-17 -->
<!-- lemma-17: body_md -->
\label{lemm_extension_reducibility}
    Assume that one of the following is satisfied:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item[(i)] $G=\mathbb G_m^t$, and $C\subset G$ is a subtorus;
        \item[(ii)] $G$ is a semiabelian variety, and $C\subset G$ is an abelian subvariety.
    \end{enumerate} Then for every homomorphism $f:C\longrightarrow G'$ of semiabelian varieties, there exists a positive integer $N$ and a homomorphism $F:G\longrightarrow G'$ such that $F|_C=[N]_{G'}\circ f$.
<!-- end lemma-17 -->
<!-- proof-49: body_md -->
It suffices to prove that there exists a homomorphism
$$\pi:G\rightarrow C$$ such that $\pi|_C=[N]_C$ for some $N>0$.
Indeed, now define $F:=f\circ\pi:G\rightarrow G'$. Then
$$F|_C=f\circ\pi|_C=f\circ [N]_C=[N]_{G'}\circ f.$$

For case (i), the existence of $\pi$ is due to the fact that any splitting subtorus is a direct factor.

For case (ii), we can obtain $\pi$ by Poincar\'e reducibility if $G$ is an abelian variety. We now give a slight generalization.

Let $A$ be the abelian quotient of $G$, and let $C_A$ be the image of $C$ in $A$. Then $C_A$ is an abelian subvariety of $A$. By Poincar\'e reducibility, there exists an abelian subvariety $D_A\subset A$ such that
$C_A+D_A=A,$ and  $C_A\cap D_A \text{ is finite}.$

Let $D$ be the preimage of $D_A$ in $G$. Then $D$ is a semiabelian subvariety of $G$, and the addition map
\begin{align*}g:C\times D&\rightarrow G,\\ (b,d)&\mapsto b+d,
\end{align*}
is an isogeny. 

Take $N=\#\ker g$. Then the homomorphism
$$[N]_C\circ\operatorname{pr}_C:C\times D\rightarrow C$$
vanishes on $\ker g$, so it factors through $g$, i.e., there exists a homomorphism
$\pi:G\rightarrow C$
such that
$$\pi\circ g=[N]_C\circ\operatorname{pr}_C$$
which implies that $\pi|_C=[N]_C$. This concludes the proof.
<!-- end proof-49 -->
<!-- proof-50: body_md -->
We proceed by induction on $m$. The case $m=1$ is trivial. Assume now $m>1$ and $B\neq 0$. After reordering the factors of $G^m$, we may suppose that $p_1(B)\neq 0.$

Put $$ B_1:=p_1(B),\text{ and } K:=(p_2,\dots,p_m)(\text{neutral component of }B\cap\ker p_1).$$Then $B_1\subset G$ is again either a subtorus of $G=\mathbb G_m^t$ or an abelian subvariety of $G$, and $K\subset G^{m-1}$ is of the same type as $B$.

Since $B$ is either a torus or an abelian variety, by Poincar\'e reducibility, there exists a homomorphism $\tau:B_1\rightarrow B$ of finite kernel, and an integer $n>0$ such that \begin{equation}\label{eq_poincare_reduce}
    (p_1|_{B})\circ\tau=[n]_{B_1}.
\end{equation} Indeed, we may replace $\tau$ by its composition with a quasi-inverse of \( (p_1|_{B})\circ \tau\).

Let $\sigma:=(p_2,\dots,p_m)\circ\tau:B_1\rightarrow G^{m-1}$. Then $ \tau(a)=(na,\sigma(a))$
for $a\in B_1.$
By Lemma \ref{lemm_extension_reducibility}, there exist $M>0$ and a homomorphism $\varphi:G\rightarrow G^{m-1}$
such that $\varphi|_{B_1}=[M]_{G^{m-1}}\circ \sigma.$

Define the automorphism
\begin{align*}
    h_0:G^m&\rightarrow G^m\\
    (x_1,x_2,\dots, x_m)&\mapsto (Mnx_1,Mn(x_2,\dots, x_m)-\varphi(x_1))  
\end{align*}
Then $h_0$ preserves every subgroup $\ker(p_1,\ldots,p_i)$ for $i=1,\dots, m$.

For any $a\in B_1$, set $k:=na-\tau(p_1(a))\in B$. Then $p_1(k)=0$ by \eqref{eq_poincare_reduce}, i.e., $k\in \mathrm{ker}(p_1)\cap B.$ Therefore \begin{align*}h_0(a)&=Mna-(0,\varphi(p_1(a)))\\&=Mna-(0,M\sigma(p_1(a)))\\&=Mna-(0,M(p_2,\dots,p_m)(\tau(p_1(a))))\\
&=Mna+(0,M(p_2,\dots,p_m)(k-na))\\
&=Mna-Mn(p_2,\cdots,p_m)(a)+Mk\\
&=Mn(p_1(a),0)+Mk,
\end{align*}
which implies that $(p_2,\dots, p_m)(h_0(B))\subset (p_2,\dots,p_m)(\mathrm{ker}(p_1)\cap B)$. For dimension reasons, we must have $h_0(B)= B\times K.$

Applying the induction hypothesis to $K\subset G^{m-1},$
after reordering the last $m-1$ factors of $G^m$, there exists an isogeny
\[
h':G^{m-1}\longrightarrow G^{m-1}
\]
such that
\begin{itemize}
    \item $h'(K)=K_2\times\cdots\times K_m,$ where $K_i=p_i(h'(K)),$ and $K_i\neq 0$ exactly for $i\le m'\leq m.$
    \item $h'$ preserves subgroups $\ker(p_2,\dots, p_i)$ for $i=1,\dots, m-1$. Note that here we number the factors of $G^{m-1}$ by $2,\dots, m$. Moreover, the induced isogeny $h'^{(m')}=h'|_{\ker(p_2,\dots, p_{m'})}=[n']_{G^{m-m'}}$ for some $n'>0$.
    \item For each $i=2,\dots, m$ there exists an isogeny $h'_i:G\rightarrow G$ such that 
        $$h'_i\circ p_{i}= p_{i}\circ h'^{(i-1)}.$$
\end{itemize}
Define
\[
h:=(\mathrm{id}_G\times h')\circ h_0.
\]
Then
\[
h(B)=(\mathrm{id}_G\times h')(B_1\times K)=B_1\times K_2\times\cdots\times K_m.
\]
For $i\ge 2$, put $B_i:=K_i$. We thus obtain (1) and (2).

Notice that $$h^{(i)}=(\mathrm{id_G}\times h')\circ [Mn]_{\ker(p_1,\dots,p_i)}=[Mn]_{G^{m-i}}\circ h'^{(i)}$$
for $i=1,\dots,m-1$, which proves (3) and (4) after putting $h_1=[Mn]_G$ and $h_i=[Mn]_G\circ h_i'$ for $i=2,\dots, m$.
<!-- end proof-50 -->
